title: session-fragmentation-pocket-brief-may19-2028
content:
Quick snapshot / working notes: session fragmentation, tail spikes, and cost pockets (rough).

Goal: produce a compact reference for console/product to explain why small, long-lived sessions blow up p99 cost and which knobs meaningfully move the needle.

Background/intuition
- We see a class of customer workloads: low steady QPS but high session churn and long history per session. Small interleaved turns -> many KV cache misses -> repeated KV reloads -> short bursts of GPU work per request with poor amortization.
- Outcome: high p99, high dollars-per-1k-queries even at low average CPU/GPU utilization. This doc ties numbers to knobs and quick tradeoffs for product collateral.

Test matrix (short)
- Model: open-llama-13b-quant-v2 (representative), seq-len cap 2048.
- HW: A100-40GB equiv slot, single-GPU worker config used for parity with other bench notes.
- Scenarios:
  1) Steady-stream: 100 qps sustained, avg session length 3 turns, avg tokens/turn 25.
  2) Microburst: background 20 qps, occasional bursts 400 qps for 5–15s (10s typical), sessions short.
  3) Sessionized-long: 5 qps overall but 6k active sessions each with 30-turn history; inter-turn spacing 30–120s.
  4) Sparse-high-history: 1 qps global with 20k sessions, median history 200 tokens, lots of KV misses.

Methodology notes
- Each scenario run for 30 minutes (except sparse which ran 2 hours to capture rare tail events).
- Observed metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), tokens-per-query, observed KV cache hit-rate, GPU active duty-cycle, dollars per 1k queries (amortized using our cost model: $X per GPU-hour ported from infra sheet), and estimated cold-penalty component (ms).
- Synthetic client simulates realistic think times; no client-side retries to isolate server tails.

Results (annotated table)
Scenario | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | kv-hit | tokens/q | $/1k
---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:
Steady-stream | 72 | 120 | 230 | 0.86 | 25 | 1.6
Microburst | 85 | 170 | 540 | 0.80 | 26 | 3.1
Sessionized-long | 95 | 210 | 980 | 0.32 | 28 | 12.4
Sparse-high-history | 110 | 360 | 2200 | 0.18 | 30 | 21.8

Interpretation / highlights
- KV cache hit-rate is the dominant explanatory variable for p99 differences here. When hit-rate drops below ~40% p99 escalates non-linearly due to repeated KV materialization overhead.
- Cost per 1k queries skyrockets in low-hit scenarios despite low average GPU duty-cycle — wasted per-request setup is expensive.
- Microbursts increase p99 compared to steady but the damage is modest if KV-hit stays high; the worst case is when microbursts coincide with low hit-rate (e.g., after a cache eviction window).

Text chart: p99 across scenarios (normalized, bigger is worse)
- Steady-stream: ███░░░ (230ms)
- Microburst: █████░░ (540ms)
- Sessionized-long: ██████████░ (980ms)
- Sparse-high-history: █████████████████ (2200ms)

Quick knob experiments (what moved the needle)
- Aggressive prefix caching (extend retention window by 3x): raised kv-hit ~+0.28 absolute for sessionized-long -> p99 dropped ~520ms (from 980 to ~460ms), $/1k down ~50%.
- Batching window increase from 8ms to 25ms: helps throughput but increases p50 by ~15ms; p99 improved slightly in microburst but not in sparse-high-history where KV cost dominates.
- Lightweight warm pools (1 prewarmed worker per 1000 sessions): reduced cold-penalty component but only effective if sessions are pinned; savings were marginal for sparse-high-history because materialization itself dominates.

Unresolved / TODOs
- Need to run same matrix on an fp16 70B candidate for relative multiplicative factors (are kv costs proportional?). Jira: INF-2742
- Validate cost model with real dedicated cluster pricing (this sheet uses a placeholder $X/hr number).
- Check interaction with network egress when KV objects live in remote cache (Rina to follow up).

Suggested wording for a slide (short):
- Headline: "Session fragmentation creates hidden per-request setup costs";
- Bullets:
  • Low average utilization can mask very high unit costs when KV-hit is low.
  • Small session turns and long histories are a perfect storm: repeated rehydration + low amortization.
  • Remedies: extend retention, conservative batching, and session-aware warm pools.

Slack-links / references (working)
- #runtime-bench: thread "kv-hit shock" (Mar 28) — see snippets
- INF-2742 (Jira) has experiment spec + workload generator
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1398 contains the retention-window change used in the quick-knob test

Bottom line (one-liner):
- For session-heavy apps, prioritize cache retention and session-aware warm pools — they reduce p99 and dollars-per-1k far more than naive batching or prewarming alone.

Notes-to-self: save csvs to s3://redwood-bench/session-frag/may19/ and mark for product review. Consider a short one-pager for sales that translates $/1k into customer-facing monthly spend examples.
